Key Takeaways

  • Drop your reader straight into the action — avoid slow, generic openings. Start with tension, emotion, or a question.
  • Shift between time, mood, tone, or perspective to keep your writing dynamic and show the examiner you are in control.
  • Zoom in and out to vary your focus — wide-angle descriptions of setting and close-up details of objects or characters create a cinematic effect.
  • Link your ending back to your opening with a repeated image or phrase, but change something to show development.

Key Takeaways

  • Question 3 is worth 8 marks and assesses your ability to analyse structural features (not language) across the whole text, linking every point to the specific focus of the question.
  • Use correct subject terminology — foreshadowing, pivotal point, shifts in focus, narrative pace, juxtaposition, anti-climax — and explain how each structural choice creates a specific effect on the reader.
  • Quality beats quantity: 2–3 well-developed analytical paragraphs will score higher than five shallow observations. The mark scheme rewards depth, not the number of points you make.

Key Takeaways

  • The “Big 5” language techniques — metaphor, personification, simile, hyperbole, and adjectives/adverbs — appear in almost every fiction extract and are the techniques examiners most commonly reward.
  • Naming the technique is not enough. You must explain its effect on the reader and explore the connotations of key words to move beyond Level 2.
  • Quality beats quantity: 2–3 detailed, perceptive points will outscore 5 shallow observations every time.

Key Takeaways

  • Letters need a salutation, formal or informal register matched to the audience, and an appropriate sign-off. Articles need a headline, an engaging opening, and clear paragraphs linked by discourse markers.
  • Tone, style, and register must be consistently matched to your purpose and audience throughout your response — this is the difference between Level 2 and Level 3 on the AO5 mark scheme.
  • Leave time to proofread. AO6 is worth 16 marks — varied punctuation, sentence forms, and accurate spelling can push your grade up significantly.

Key Takeaways

  • A countdown narrative builds tension around a ticking clock, giving your story natural structure, pace variation, and urgency — all of which are rewarded at Level 4 by the AQA mark scheme.
  • Use the five-stage model (establish the clock, slow tension, the shift, the rush, the moment) as a planning framework for any creative writing prompt.
  • Quality beats quantity: vary your sentence forms deliberately, use ambitious vocabulary with purpose, and always proofread — AO6 (technical accuracy) is worth 16 of the 40 marks.

Key Takeaways

  • Match form, audience and purpose. A speech must sound like a speech (direct address, rhetorical devices, call to action). An essay must be formal, structured and balanced. The mark scheme rewards writing that is “assuredly matched to purpose and audience.”
  • Plan before you write. Decide your viewpoint, generate 3–4 clear points, choose your devices, and plan your opening and closing. A planned response is always more coherent and convincing.
  • Technical accuracy is worth 16 marks. Vary your punctuation, use a range of sentence forms, spell ambitiously but accurately, and always proofread. These marks are the most reliable way to boost your grade.

Key Takeaways

  • Structure in non-fiction includes openings, shifts in tone or pace, sentence forms, paragraph sequencing, and endings — all of which can be analysed for their effect on the reader.
  • Sentence forms (short declarative sentences, long flowing sentences, rhetorical questions) are explicitly included in the AQA mark scheme for Question 3. Always link form to effect.
  • Comparing structural choices in Question 4 is an underused but highly effective approach that demonstrates sophisticated understanding and creates like-for-like comparisons.
